hook: You know Jesus said no one has greater love than to die for friends. But did you know he said it on the night he was arrested?
story:
It was night. Judas had taken the piece of bread and gone out, and the others were left at the table with a Lord who had just told them that one of them would betray him. John says plainly that Jesus was “troubled in spirit” and that the disciples “looked at one another, perplexed”.

This is the supper where Jesus had already washed their feet, having “loved them to the end”. Now he talks, and what he says is startling. He tells them they are no longer servants, because “the servant doesn’t know what his lord does.” Instead, “I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” The Greek word for friend here, philos, is the word for someone held dear and close, and a few verses later it is set against the word for a servant.

Somewhere in that room was a man who had already promised, “I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus had answered him with a question: “Will you lay down your life for me?” Now, to all of them, he gives the measure of love: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.”

Then John moves quickly. “When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples” to a garden across the brook Kidron. Judas arrived with soldiers, officers, lanterns and torches. Jesus stepped forward and asked whom they wanted. When they said Jesus of Nazareth, he answered, “If therefore you seek me, let these go their way,” and John adds that this was so that the word might be fulfilled, “Of those whom you have given me, I have lost none.” When Peter drew a sword, Jesus told him to put it away.

The friends went. Mark records it in a few words: “They all left him, and fled.” Then John tells of the cross: Jesus went out, bearing his cross, to the place called Golgotha, where they crucified him. The one who had spoken about laying down a life for friends did it.

moment:
Jesus is not speaking in the abstract. The words come in the middle of a longer talk about remaining in his love, and just before this verse he gives his command: “love one another, even as I have loved you.” The verse then says what that love looks like at its greatest. Right after it comes a condition that people sometimes skip: “You are my friends if you do whatever I command you.”

The listeners are not strangers. They are the disciples who had walked with him, and a few verses on he tells them the world will hate them as it hated him. That same night, soldiers come to the garden, and the speaker is bound.
around:
Earlier in this same Gospel Jesus said, “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” He also said that no one takes his life from him: “I lay it down by myself.” So when he speaks of laying down a life for friends at the table, this Gospel has already shown him saying it about himself.

The verse also sits beside a surprising line from Paul. In Romans, Paul says someone might hardly die even for a righteous man, and then adds that “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Jesus calls his listeners friends here. Paul says the love reached people who were still enemies. Readers can hold the two together.
after:
The disciples who ran did not stay scattered. Peter, who had promised to lay down his life, later stood up in Jerusalem and preached. Stephen was stoned for his testimony, and as he died he asked, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” Luke says Herod “killed James, the brother of John, with the sword”. A letter in the same New Testament, 1 John, says, “we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.”

The verse has traveled far outside the church. When the Unknown Warrior was buried in Westminster Abbey on November 11, 1920, it was carved into his grave, and the Abbey says that no one knows who he was. On February 3, 1943, the troop ship Dorchester was torpedoed in the North Atlantic. According to the U.S. Army, four chaplains, a Methodist minister, a rabbi, a Catholic priest and a Dutch Reformed minister, gave their life jackets to others, then linked arms on the deck, singing hymns and prayers as it sank. Congress authorized a Special Medal for Heroism for them, presented to their families in 1961.

In August 1941 at Auschwitz, Maximilian Kolbe, a Franciscan priest, stepped forward to take the place of a man who cried out for his wife and child. The sources say Kolbe was the last of the ten men left alive in the bunker after two weeks, and that he was killed with an injection on August 14. The man he replaced, Franciszek Gajowniczek, lived until 1995 and was at Kolbe’s canonization in 1982.
readings:
One common reading hears this verse first as Jesus describing his own death. He says it on the night he is arrested, he goes to the cross, and his friends are the ones he calls to “love one another, even as I have loved you.”

Others hear it as a sentence that is true of any person, and its first words are cut into the stone around the grave of the Unknown Warrior. The wording in the verse is general, “someone lay down his life”, and nothing in it limits who may do so.

A third reading asks whether the verse is a command or a description. It is placed right after a command to love, and 1 John later draws the line out for believers. But it does not say that anyone must die. Readers differ on how much weight to put on each side, and the text leaves room for all three readings.
argued:
People have turned to this verse for those who gave their lives. When the Dorchester went down in 1943, Dr. Mark W. Johnson, the Army Chaplain Corps historian, wrote that the four chaplains who gave away their life jackets stayed by choice: [[johnson]] He adds that they knowingly sealed their fates.

In 1920, on the card King George V laid on the coffin of the Unknown Warrior, he wrote: [[king-george]] The Abbey carved the first words of the verse around the grave.

When Pope John Paul II canonized Maximilian Kolbe in 1982, he did so as a martyr. Father James McCurry, who led a pilgrimage to Rome for the Mass, says that had been in question, because Kolbe was killed not for his faith but for giving his place to another man. The old rule, as he states it, is strict: [[mccurry]] He adds that Kolbe died putting his faith into the practice of heroic charity.
point: The verse is a measure of love, and it is spoken to friends. Jesus gives it on the night the soldiers come, to people about to run, and then he does what he said. The verse is not a demand that anyone die. It says what love looks like when it costs everything.
lesson:
You may never face a night like the garden. Most of love is quieter: the time you give up, the seat you give away, the call you make when you would rather rest.

But notice who Jesus is talking to. He does not say it to people who have earned it. He says it to a table of perplexed friends, one of whom will deny him and most of whom will leave. The love he describes was not waiting for them to be ready.

If you want to live this verse, you can begin small and close. Who is a friend, a neighbor or someone in your family that you could carry this week? You can also read John 15 in one sitting and pray over just the first twelve verses. And if you do not share this faith, the lives of Kolbe and the four chaplains still ask a question worth sitting with: what would it look like to love someone more than your own safety?

echoes.note: Jesus had said it about himself before he said it to friends: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” The love in John 15 is the same one.
Paul says that “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” Where John 15 speaks of friends, Paul shows the same love reaching people who were far from him.
A later letter turns the verse toward its readers: “we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” It does so by pointing back to what Christ had already done.
